tagline: Coworkers point AI at real work, and a person still says yes.
sticker: AI changes wait for a person's yes

solved.did: Set it up so every AI change shows a preview and waits for a yes before it touches the store.
solved.ended: That goes for the buyer's own AI too.

solved.problem: The support chatbot was reading old text left behind in the website's pages.
solved.did: Found the leftovers and cleared them out.
solved.ended: Its answers now come from what customers can actually see.

solved.problem: Purchasing wanted to use their own AI on live numbers without breaking anything.

worksWith: Purchasing, customer service and support, finance, leadership, a developer.
story: Coworkers use their own AI against live numbers now. Purchasing can build on their data, support can look up an order, and product-page changes wait for a person to approve them.
Giving an assistant access meant deciding what it could read and what it could change.

So I set the rule: an AI shows what it wants to change, and nothing changes until someone confirms it. Each tool and each machine got its own key, limited to one job, so one mistake never reaches everything. Wherever the AI only needs to look, it can only look.
I wrote a guide their assistant could read cold: what is live, what is read-only, what needs a yes. I kept it current and checked it against what the systems really do.
The smaller jobs stayed useful too: turning a design into page code, checking the voice of a draft, or reading a script aloud before the real recording.
